Transform parameterization In this section we give additional details on the three components that make up the overall diffeomorphism TS→V that maps the idealized spiral in canonical space to the highly deformed shape observed in the scan volume. The transform is a composition TS→V = Taff ◦Tflow ◦Tgap, where: (i) Taff is a per-slice affine (scaling and translation) transform; (ii) Tflow is the result of integrating a flow field; (iii) Tgap rescales inter-winding gaps. A.1. Per-slice affine transform We non-isotropically scale and translate each slice in the xy-plane; the scale factors and translations vary wrt z. This stage is parameterized by N 2D log-scales and translations where N is a fixed number of keypoints along the z-axis; the translations and log-scales are linearly interpolated for other z values. Thus, for a given point x = (x1, x2, x3), we have T_\ma t h r m {aff}(\ m at hb f {x}) = \ le f t (\begin {array}{c} x_1 \exp (s_1) + t_1 \\ x_2 \exp (s_2) + t_2 \\ x_3 \end {array} \right ) where (s1, s2) = (1−α) s(⌊τ⌋)+α s(⌊t⌋+1), α = τ −⌊τ⌋, τ = N(x3 −zmin)/(zmax −zmin), and S(n), n = 1 . . . N are the N log-scales; translations are defined analogously. A.2. Integrated flow field We introduce a flow velocity field u, i.e. a 3D vector field of 3D velocities defined over the scan volume. This allows us to transform a given point by simulating its movement in flow of the given local velocities for a fixed length of time. This is done by solving an ODE defined by u and an initial condition (the starting point). Writing ϕ(t) for the transform induced by simulating the flow u for time t, the final transformed position of a point x is given by Tflow(x) = ϕ(1)(x), where ϕ(t) evolves according to \frac {d } { d t}\phi ^{(t)}(\mathbf {x}) = \mathbf {u}\left ( \phi ^{(t)}(\mathbf {x}) \right ) with the initial condition ϕ(0)(x) = x, i.e. we start with an identity transform. The resulting transformation is guaranteed to be a diffeomorphism, provided the flow field u is itself smooth [4, 5]. Formally, the space of flow fields is the Lie algebra that generates the Lie group of diffeomorphisms; the former provides a straightforward way to parameterize the latter. Moreover, the inverse diffeomorphism is easily found by negating the flow field, then integrating backwards in time. We define the velocity field as the sum two underlying fields u = ucoarse + ufine, where ucoarse is more spatially smooth than ufine. Both fields are defined by trilinear interpolation of explicitly-represented discrete grids of 3D velocity vectors. The grid for ufine is 48× lower resolution than the original CT volume, and that for ucoarse is a further 6× lower. We solve the ODE using explicit Euler integration with 16 steps; more steps did not result in significantly different results, whereas fewer could cause TS→V ◦TV→S to not be sufficiently close to the identity transform. Experiments with scale-and-square integration [32]—which requires fewer operations—showed that it is less stable in our setting than Euler integration. To update the flow field via gradient descent, we must differentiate back through the ODE solve, i.e. compute the Jacobian of ϕ(1)(x) wrt u. We achieve this by directly unrolling and back-propagating through the Euler updates; this is tractable due to the relatively small number of steps. With more steps or larger minibatches, it would become preferable to use the adjoint method, similar to continuous normalizing flows [12]. We also conducted initial experiments using a timevarying velocity field, defined explicitly by changing the 3D coarse and fine grids to be 4D. This has only a minor effect on compute cost but increases memory linearly with the number of timesteps. Despite such fields having intuitively simpler behavior, we did not notice any significant improvements to final results, hence all our main experiments use a time-constant field. We also tested an implicit velocity field defined by a small neural network (a residual MLP) operating on 3D coordinates in the volume, and regressing these directly to the velocity vector, similar to neural radiance fields (NeRF)

[30] and other neural field methods [66]. While this potentially allows allocating parameter capacity more efficiently where needed (instead of uniformly across the volume regardless of curvature), in practice we found the computational expense to be prohibitive. A.3. Inter-winding gap scaling We define a scalar field over the 2D surface of the canonical scroll spiral, which specifies for each point, by how much the next winding should be pushed outward from its default distance (defined by being an Archimedean spiral), i.e. locally scaling the gaps between windings. Since this field is defined only on the 2D spiral surface (truncated at a certain number of windings), it has quadratic cost in memory. This allows using a finer resolution than the full-volume flow field, and is also more expressive since it can directly separate or push apart nearby sheets regardless of how their position relates to the fixed flow-field grids. The field itself is defined explicitly by scalar values on a 2D grid wrt the z and θ coordinates of eq. 1 in the main paper. This discrete representation is extended to the 2D plane by bilinear interpolation. The field values are interpreted as log scale factors multiplying the spacing between windings, originally defined by the global winding rate ω. Specifically, for a given point x, we find the next spiral winding inwards from it, measure the radial distance to that winding, multiply this distance by the relevant scale factor, and move the point outwards correspondingly. Additional Visualizations Figure 7a shows cross-sections of PHerc. Paris 4, with the original undeformed spiral (before optimization) overlaid (top), and the fitted version (bottom). We also display (Figure 7b) two slices that are transformed by the inverse diffeomorphism to map them back into canonical space, resulting in near-circular concentric windings. Similarly, Figure 8 shows cross-sections of PHerc. 172 before and after fitting, while Figure 9 shows undeformed slices with circularized windings. In Figure 10 we show the full unrolling of PHerc. 172 produced by our method. In Figures 11–17 we zoom in on parts of the unwrapped surface, with enhanced contrast. In each of these views, ink is visible forming Greek characters (light against the darker background) and sometimes complete words. Note also the individual fibers of papyrus visible forming continuous lines through the view, indicating the our method is correctly following the true sheet surfaces. (a) (b) Figure 7.
